title: Stylistics
subtitle: How a sentence sounds like someone: rhythm, lexical choice, distance — and how to borrow, bend or rebuild a manner at will

lessons.title: Le style et la voix
lessons.description: What actually makes a personal style: the rhythm of the sentence, the lexical register a writer keeps returning to, and the distance held from the subject.

blocks.heading: Le rythme : la première signature
blocks.body: Before a reader notices your vocabulary, they hear your rhythm. French stylistics distinguishes « la parataxe » — short clauses juxtaposed, often without conjunctions — from « l'hypotaxe », where subordinate clauses hang from a main clause and build a long balanced « période ». Neither is better; each produces an effect. Parataxis accelerates, fragments, and lets the reader draw the links; hypotaxis subordinates, hierarchises, and tells the reader exactly which idea depends on which.

examples.french: Il est entré. Il n'a rien dit. Il a posé les clés sur la table.
examples.english: He came in. He said nothing. He put the keys on the table.
examples.note: parataxe : three blocks, no connector — the reader supplies the causality

examples.french: Comme il n'avait rien à dire et que la nuit avait été longue, il posa les clés sur la table sans même ôter son manteau.
examples.english: Since he had nothing to say and the night had been long, he set the keys on the table without even taking off his coat.
examples.note: hypotaxe : the same scene, hierarchised — one main clause, everything else subordinate

examples.french: Sa phrase est courte, nerveuse, presque haletante.
examples.english: His sentence is short, tense, almost breathless.
examples.note: the rhythm of the description imitates what it describes

examples.french: Il écrit par vagues : la phrase enfle, se déploie, retombe.
examples.english: He writes in waves: the sentence swells, unfurls, subsides.
examples.note: « le souffle » — the long sweep of a sentence that carries several beats

examples.french: Un ternaire bien placé donne à la période son point d'appui.
examples.english: A well-placed ternary rhythm gives the periodic sentence its footing.
examples.note: groups of three remain the most audible rhythmic unit in French prose

blocks.tip: Read your paragraph aloud and mark where you breathe. If you never breathe, the reader never rests; if you breathe every four words, the text stumbles. Style is largely the management of that breath.

blocks.heading: Le lexique : ce que l'on choisit sans y penser
blocks.body: A writer's lexicon is rarely a conscious decision — it is a set of habits. Some authors reach systematically for concrete nouns, others for abstractions; some keep a « champ lexical » running for pages (water, machinery, illness) so that the whole text is quietly coloured. The revealing detail is repetition: a word that returns three times in a page is a signature, whether the writer meant it or not.

examples.french: Chez elle, tout est verbe : on court, on cogne, on recommence.
examples.english: With her, everything is verbs: you run, you knock, you start again.
examples.note: verb-driven prose reads as energy; noun-driven prose reads as analysis

examples.french: Il file un champ lexical marin sur trois pages : houle, dérive, naufrage.
examples.english: He runs a nautical lexical field for three pages: swell, drift, shipwreck.
examples.note: « filer » a lexical field = keeping it going deliberately

examples.french: Son idiolecte se reconnaît à deux mots : « or » et « précisément ».
examples.english: You can recognise his idiolect from two words: “now” and “precisely”.
examples.note: l'idiolecte = the individual's own private dialect

examples.french: Elle bannit les adverbes en -ment ; c'est un parti pris, pas un hasard.
examples.english: She bans -ly adverbs; it is a deliberate stance, not chance.
examples.note: what a style refuses defines it as much as what it uses

examples.french: Le mot juste vaut mieux que trois mots approchants.
examples.english: The right word is worth more than three approximate ones.
examples.note: the classic French stylistic creed, from Flaubert onwards

blocks.tip: Take any page you have written and list every noun. If the list looks like a dictionary of abstractions — situation, élément, aspect, niveau — your style has no body yet.

blocks.heading: La distance : où se tient celui qui parle
blocks.body: The third variable is distance: how close the speaking voice stands to what it describes. A narrator can be inside a character's head (free indirect style), at their shoulder, or high above with the cold eye of a report. French marks this distance through tense, through modalisation (« sans doute », « paraît-il ») and above all through irony, which is distance made audible.

examples.french: Il était, paraît-il, un homme remarquable.
examples.english: He was, so they say, a remarkable man.
examples.note: « paraît-il » inserts distance: the narrator declines to vouch for it

examples.french: Quelle chance il avait eue ! Enfin quelqu'un l'écoutait.
examples.english: What luck he had had! At last someone was listening to him.
examples.note: style indirect libre — the narrator borrows the character's voice without quotation marks

examples.french: Le sujet a manifesté une certaine irritation.
examples.english: The subject displayed a certain irritation.
examples.note: maximum distance: the clinical register of a report

examples.french: On l'aurait dit heureux ; il ne l'était pas.
examples.english: You would have thought him happy; he was not.
examples.note: the narrator corrects the reader — a very controlled, slightly ironic distance

examples.french: Elle prend du recul et son ironie devient tendresse.
examples.english: She steps back and her irony turns into tenderness.
examples.note: distance is not coldness: the same recul can produce affection

blocks.tip: Change nothing but the distance and the text changes genre. The same funeral, told from inside, at the shoulder, or from a police report, gives you an elegy, a novel, or a satire.

items.example: Son style se reconnaît dès la première ligne.
items.exampleEnglish: His style is recognisable from the very first line.

items.example: Elle a mis dix ans à trouver sa voix.
items.exampleEnglish: It took her ten years to find her voice.

items.example: Le ton du texte est faussement détaché.
items.exampleEnglish: The tone of the text is deceptively detached.

items.example: La tonalité générale du recueil est mélancolique.
items.exampleEnglish: The general key of the collection is melancholy.

items.example: Le rythme s'accélère dès que le personnage ment.
items.exampleEnglish: The rhythm speeds up as soon as the character lies.

items.example: Ses phrases retombent toujours sur la même cadence.
items.exampleEnglish: His sentences always come to rest on the same cadence.

items.example: Cette page a un souffle que la précédente n'avait pas.
items.exampleEnglish: This page has a sweep the previous one lacked.

items.example: La période classique se déploie puis se referme sur une chute brève.
items.exampleEnglish: The classical periodic sentence unfolds, then closes on a short fall.

items.example: La parataxe donne au récit une allure de constat.
items.exampleEnglish: Parataxis gives the narrative the feel of a statement of fact.

items.example: L'hypotaxe hiérarchise ce que la parataxe se contente de poser.
items.exampleEnglish: Hypotaxis ranks what parataxis merely sets down.

items.example: Sa syntaxe est tordue, mais jamais fautive.
items.exampleEnglish: His syntax is twisted, but never incorrect.

items.example: Le lexique du texte reste volontairement pauvre.
items.exampleEnglish: The text's lexicon is deliberately kept sparse.

items.example: Il file un champ lexical de la maladie sur tout le chapitre.
items.exampleEnglish: He runs a lexical field of illness through the whole chapter.

items.example: La distance du narrateur rend la scène supportable.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrator's distance makes the scene bearable.

items.example: Elle raconte son enfance avec un recul désarmant.
items.exampleEnglish: She tells of her childhood with disarming detachment.

items.example: La sobriété de la description en fait toute la force.
items.exampleEnglish: The restraint of the description is exactly what makes it powerful.

items.example: On admire l'ampleur de la phrase sans en perdre le fil.
items.exampleEnglish: One admires the breadth of the sentence without losing its thread.

items.example: Sa brièveté n'est jamais de la sécheresse.
items.exampleEnglish: His brevity is never dryness.

items.example: La concision s'obtient à la relecture, jamais au premier jet.
items.exampleEnglish: Conciseness is achieved at the rereading stage, never in the first draft.

items.example: Le dépouillement de son écriture désarçonne les lecteurs pressés.
items.exampleEnglish: The bareness of his writing throws hurried readers off.

items.example: Il parle sans emphase, ce qui rend ses mots plus lourds.
items.exampleEnglish: He speaks without grandiloquence, which makes his words weigh more.

items.example: Sa préciosité finit par lasser dès la deuxième page.
items.exampleEnglish: His affectation ends up tiring you by the second page.

items.example: Chaque idiolecte tient à trois ou quatre habitudes de langue.
items.exampleEnglish: Every idiolect comes down to three or four habits of language.

items.example: Cette tournure sent son dix-neuvième siècle.
items.exampleEnglish: That turn of phrase reeks of the nineteenth century.

items.example: Le procédé est visible, donc il ne fonctionne plus.
items.exampleEnglish: The device is visible, so it no longer works.

items.example: Une inflexion suffit pour faire basculer la phrase dans l'ironie.
items.exampleEnglish: One inflection is enough to tip the sentence into irony.

items.example: « En fait » est devenu chez lui un tic de langage.
items.exampleEnglish: “Actually” has become a verbal tic with him.

items.example: La scansion en trois temps donne au discours son autorité.
items.exampleEnglish: The three-beat scansion gives the speech its authority.

items.example: Il cisèle ses fins de chapitre pendant des semaines.
items.exampleEnglish: He chisels his chapter endings for weeks.

items.example: Affûtez vos verbes avant de toucher aux adjectifs.
items.exampleEnglish: Sharpen your verbs before you touch the adjectives.

items.english: to weigh down, to make heavy
items.example: Ces incises alourdissent une phrase déjà longue.
items.exampleEnglish: These interpolated clauses weigh down an already long sentence.

items.example: Resserrez le paragraphe : il dit deux fois la même chose.
items.exampleEnglish: Tighten the paragraph: it says the same thing twice.

items.example: Un style ampoulé cache souvent une pensée courte.
items.exampleEnglish: A bombastic style often hides a short thought.

items.example: Il s'exprime dans une langue châtiée, même à table.
items.exampleEnglish: He expresses himself in polished language, even at the dinner table.

items.example: Son phrasé heurté épouse l'angoisse du personnage.
items.exampleEnglish: His jerky phrasing matches the character's anxiety.

items.example: Une prose fluide n'est pas forcément une prose facile.
items.exampleEnglish: Flowing prose is not necessarily easy prose.

items.example: Le récit avance sur un ton feutré, presque chuchoté.
items.exampleEnglish: The narrative advances in a hushed, almost whispered tone.

blocks.heading: Le style indirect libre
blocks.body: Free indirect style lets a narrator speak a character's thoughts in the third person, with no « il pensa que » and no quotation marks. Keep the tense of narration (imparfait, plus-que-parfait, conditionnel as future-in-the-past) but import the character's vocabulary, exclamations and questions. It is the single most efficient way to control distance: the voice is simultaneously outside and inside.

examples.french: Il regarda la porte. Non, il n'irait pas. Pourquoi se serait-il excusé ?
examples.english: He looked at the door. No, he would not go. Why should he have apologised?
examples.note: « n'irait pas » = conditional as future-in-the-past; the question is the character's, not the narrator's

examples.french: Elle rangea ses affaires. Demain, tout serait différent.
examples.english: She put away her things. Tomorrow everything would be different.
examples.note: « demain » kept as the character says it, not converted to « le lendemain »

examples.french: Il pensa qu'il n'irait pas et qu'il n'avait pas à s'excuser.
examples.english: He thought that he would not go and that he did not have to apologise.
examples.note: the same content in ordinary indirect speech — flatter, more distant

examples.french: Quelle idée, aussi, d'avoir accepté !
examples.english: What an idea, too, to have accepted!
examples.note: « aussi » in this position is spoken French — the character's own tone leaking in

examples.french: Le vieil homme haussa les épaules. Ces gens-là ne changeraient jamais.
examples.english: The old man shrugged. Those people would never change.
examples.note: « ces gens-là » carries his contempt without the narrator endorsing it

blocks.tip: Test: can you insert « pensa-t-il » without changing a single word? If yes, you are in free indirect style.

blocks.heading: Ordre des mots et mise en relief
blocks.body: French word order is less free than in many languages, so writers get emphasis from dislocation and from cleft constructions. « C'est … que / qui » highlights one element; a dislocated noun with a resumptive pronoun (« Ce livre, je l'ai lu ») fronts a topic; inversion after certain adverbs (à peine, aussi, peut-être, ainsi) raises the register instantly.

examples.french: C'est ce silence-là qui m'a inquiété, pas ses paroles.
examples.english: It was that silence that worried me, not his words.
examples.note: cleft with « qui » — the highlighted element is the subject

examples.french: Ce livre, je l'ai lu trois fois sans le comprendre.
examples.english: That book, I read it three times without understanding it.
examples.note: left dislocation + resumptive « l' » — spoken French, but usable in prose for topic-setting

examples.french: À peine était-il sorti que le téléphone sonna.
examples.english: Hardly had he gone out when the telephone rang.
examples.note: inversion after « à peine » — literary and instantly formal

examples.french: Peut-être avons-nous mal lu ce texte.
examples.english: Perhaps we have misread this text.
examples.note: « peut-être » + inversion; « peut-être qu'on a mal lu » is the neutral version

examples.french: Ainsi s'achève une carrière commencée dans l'indifférence.
examples.english: Thus ends a career begun in indifference.
examples.note: inversion after « ainsi » gives a closing, almost oratorical fall

blocks.tip: Use one emphatic construction per paragraph at most. Stacked clefts and dislocations sound like someone shouting every word.

items.french: Il est entré. Il n'a rien dit. Il a posé les clés sur la table.
items.english: He came in. He said nothing. He put the keys on the table.
items.prompt: Read this paratactic sequence aloud, letting each full stop land.
items.tip: Drop the pitch clearly at each full stop and pause a full beat. If the three clauses run together, the parataxis is lost.

items.french: Comme il n'avait rien à dire et que la nuit avait été longue, il posa les clés sur la table sans même ôter son manteau.
items.english: Since he had nothing to say and the night had been long, he set the keys on the table without even taking off his coat.
items.prompt: Now the hypotactic version: keep the voice suspended until the main clause.
items.tip: Hold a slightly rising pitch through « longue », then let the main clause fall. Do not breathe before « il posa ».

items.french: Ce n'est pas ce qu'il dit qui me gêne, c'est la manière dont il le dit.
items.english: It is not what he says that bothers me, it is the way he says it.
items.prompt: Say this cleft sentence with the stress on the highlighted elements.
items.tip: Push slightly on « ce qu'il dit » and on « la manière » — French emphasis is carried by the construction, so keep the volume even elsewhere.

passages.title: Deux pages, deux voix
passages.french:
On m'avait confié deux manuscrits anonymes et prié de dire lequel des deux auteurs avait du style.
Le premier commençait ainsi : « La pluie tombait. La rue était vide. J'ai attendu. »
Trois phrases, onze mots, aucune conjonction : le lecteur devait relier lui-même les morceaux.
Le second ouvrait sur une période de six lignes où la pluie, la rue et l'attente se tenaient par la main, chaque proposition suspendue à la précédente, jusqu'à une chute très brève.
J'ai lu les deux à voix haute, comme on m'a appris à le faire.
Le premier respirait vite ; on l'entendait presque courir.
Le second respirait lentement, mais il ne s'essoufflait jamais : c'était un nageur, pas un sprinteur.
Ensuite j'ai compté les mots. Chez l'un, quatre-vingts pour cent de verbes et de noms concrets ; chez l'autre, une abstraction toutes les deux lignes.
Enfin j'ai cherché la distance, ce que personne ne pense à mesurer.
Le premier narrateur restait collé à son personnage : il ne savait rien de plus que lui, ni ce qui l'attendait, ni pourquoi il avait froid.
Le second se tenait très au-dessus, avec une ironie polie qui le protégeait de ce qu'il racontait.
J'ai rendu mon verdict : les deux avaient du style, et ce n'était pas le même métier.
Le premier écrivait pour qu'on voie ; le second, pour qu'on comprenne.
On m'a répondu que je n'avais pas répondu à la question.
C'était vrai. Mais la question était mal posée : on ne classe pas les voix, on les reconnaît.
passages.english:
I had been handed two anonymous manuscripts and asked to say which of the two authors had style.
The first began like this: “The rain was falling. The street was empty. I waited.”
Three sentences, eleven words, not a single conjunction: the reader had to join the pieces up himself.
The second opened on a six-line periodic sentence in which the rain, the street and the waiting held hands, each clause suspended from the one before, up to a very short fall.
I read both aloud, as I was taught to do.
The first breathed fast; you could almost hear it running.
The second breathed slowly, but it never ran out of breath: it was a swimmer, not a sprinter.
Then I counted the words. In one, eighty per cent verbs and concrete nouns; in the other, an abstraction every two lines.
Finally I looked for the distance, which nobody thinks to measure.
The first narrator stayed glued to his character: he knew no more than the character did, neither what awaited him nor why he was cold.
The second stood well above, with a polite irony that shielded him from what he was recounting.
I delivered my verdict: both had style, and it was not the same trade.
The first wrote so that we would see; the second, so that we would understand.
I was told that I had not answered the question.
That was true. But the question was badly put: you do not rank voices, you recognise them.

lessons.title: Le pastiche
lessons.description: Imitating a manner on purpose: spotting the two or three traits that make a style recognisable, then reproducing them without tipping into parody.

blocks.heading: Pastiche, parodie, plagiat : trois choses différentes
blocks.body: French criticism separates them carefully. « Le pastiche » reproduces a manner on new material, with the reader in on the game — it is an admiring exercise. « La parodie » reuses the manner to mock it or to deflate its subject. « Le plagiat » hides the borrowing and passes it off as one's own: it is a fault, not a genre. The line between pastiche and parody is drawn by intention and by how far you « forcez le trait ».

examples.french: Ce chapitre est un pastiche affectueux du roman policier des années trente.
examples.english: This chapter is an affectionate pastiche of the 1930s detective novel.
examples.note: pastiche = same manner, new content, complicity with the reader

examples.french: En parodiant le discours officiel, il en montre le vide.
examples.english: By parodying official discourse, he shows how empty it is.
examples.note: parodie = the manner is turned against itself

examples.french: Il ne cite pas ses sources : ce n'est plus un emprunt, c'est un plagiat.
examples.english: He does not cite his sources: this is no longer a borrowing, it is plagiarism.
examples.note: the difference is disclosure, not similarity

examples.french: L'exercice de style consiste à raconter la même anecdote de vingt façons.
examples.english: The exercise in style consists of telling the same anecdote twenty ways.
examples.note: a French school tradition: the content is trivial so the manner becomes visible

examples.french: À la manière de… : trois mots qui autorisent tout, à condition de le dire.
examples.english: In the manner of…: three words that allow anything, provided you say so.
examples.note: the standard heading of a declared pastiche

blocks.tip: One honest sentence — « à la manière de » — turns a suspicious resemblance into a recognised genre. Declare the model and the reader becomes your accomplice.

blocks.heading: Repérer les traits : la fiche de pastiche
blocks.body: You cannot imitate everything at once. Practised pasticheurs build a short list: average sentence length, favourite connectors, tense of narration, one or two syntactic habits, a lexical field, and a tic. Four or five traits are enough — beyond that the imitation becomes a museum piece and loses its life. The trick is to choose the traits a reader can hear, not the ones only a grammarian would notice.

examples.french: Trait n° 1 : phrases de trois à cinq mots, jamais davantage.
examples.english: Trait no. 1: sentences of three to five words, never more.
examples.note: sentence length is the most audible trait of all

examples.french: Trait n° 2 : le passé simple, systématiquement, même pour les gestes banals.
examples.english: Trait no. 2: the passé simple, systematically, even for ordinary gestures.
examples.note: tense of narration instantly dates and situates a voice

examples.french: Trait n° 3 : une incise ironique par paragraphe, jamais deux.
examples.english: Trait no. 3: one ironic aside per paragraph, never two.
examples.note: frequency matters as much as the device itself

examples.french: Trait n° 4 : les adjectifs vont par paires, et la seconde surprend.
examples.english: Trait no. 4: adjectives come in pairs, and the second one surprises.
examples.note: a habit of construction is easier to copy than a whole vocabulary

examples.french: Trait n° 5 : il commence une phrase sur deux par « Or ».
examples.english: Trait no. 5: he begins every other sentence with “Now”.
examples.note: the tic — use it sparingly or the pastiche turns into a charge

blocks.tip: Write your five traits on a card before you write a word. If you cannot state a trait in one line, it is not a trait, it is an impression.

blocks.heading: Le dosage : où le pastiche devient charge
blocks.body: A pastiche fails in two directions. Too faint, and nobody recognises the model; too heavy, and it becomes « une charge », a caricature. The French term « forcer le trait » names the tipping point exactly. Good practice: keep the model's syntax faithful and let the content be slightly, quietly wrong for it — the humour comes from the mismatch, not from exaggeration.

examples.french: Il a forcé le trait : on ne reconnaît plus l'auteur, on ne voit que le pasticheur.
examples.english: He laid it on too thick: you no longer recognise the author, only the pasticheur.
examples.note: the classic failure mode

examples.french: Le décalage vient du sujet : la grande période classique appliquée à un ticket de métro.
examples.english: The mismatch comes from the subject: the grand classical period applied to a metro ticket.
examples.note: keep the manner intact, downgrade the material

examples.french: Un clin d'œil suffit ; deux, c'est déjà de la parodie.
examples.english: One wink is enough; two, and you are already in parody.
examples.note: « le clin d'œil » = the nod to the reader

blocks.heading: Le passé simple : la marque du récit littéraire
blocks.body: Nothing signals a literary manner faster than the passé simple. In pastiche you need to produce it, not merely recognise it. Third person forms carry almost all the weight: -a / -èrent for -er verbs, -it / -irent for most -ir and -re verbs, and a family of -ut / -urent forms (il fut, il eut, il put, il voulut, il dut, il sut, il vécut). Pair it with the imparfait for background, and never mix it with the passé composé inside the same narration.

examples.french: Il entra, salua l'assemblée et se tut.
examples.english: He came in, greeted the assembly and fell silent.
examples.note: -er verbs → entra, salua; « se taire » → il se tut

examples.french: Ils descendirent sans un mot ; personne ne les retint.
examples.english: They went down without a word; no one held them back.
examples.note: descendirent (-re verb), retint (« retenir » → il retint)

examples.french: Elle voulut répondre, mais elle n'en eut pas le temps.
examples.english: She wanted to reply, but she did not have the time.
examples.note: the -ut family: voulut, eut

examples.french: La nuit tombait ; il s'assit et attendit.
examples.english: Night was falling; he sat down and waited.
examples.note: imparfait for the setting, passé simple for the events

examples.french: Il fut sans doute le dernier à savoir la vérité.
examples.english: He was doubtless the last to know the truth.
examples.note: « il fut » — irreplaceable in a literary pastiche, impossible in speech

blocks.tip: The first-person plural (nous entrâmes, nous vînmes) exists but sounds comic outside a genuine literary frame. In pastiche, stay in the third person and you will never sound accidental.

blocks.heading: L'imparfait du subjonctif : reconnaître, doser
blocks.body: The imperfect subjunctive is dead in speech and alive in pastiche. It follows a past main verb where modern French simply uses the present subjunctive. Forms are built on the passé simple: qu'il entrât, qu'il finît, qu'il fût, qu'il eût, qu'il pût. In a pastiche of classical or nineteenth-century prose, one or two occurrences per page are enough; more, and you have written a charge instead of a pastiche.

examples.french: Il fallait qu'elle partît avant l'aube.
examples.english: She had to leave before dawn.
examples.note: modern French: « qu'elle parte » — the imperfect subjunctive dates the sentence at once

examples.french: Je craignais qu'il ne fût déjà trop tard.
examples.english: I feared it might already be too late.
examples.note: « ne » explétif + fût: the full classical apparatus

examples.french: Bien qu'il eût tout prévu, il perdit son calme.
examples.english: Although he had foreseen everything, he lost his composure.
examples.note: plus-que-parfait du subjonctif — the past of the same register

examples.french: Elle attendit qu'il finît sa phrase.
examples.english: She waited for him to finish his sentence.
examples.note: note the circumflex: finît, never finit, in the subjunctive

examples.french: Il aurait voulu qu'on le crût sur parole.
examples.english: He would have liked to be taken at his word.
examples.note: « qu'on le crût » (croire) — reserved for deliberate archaism

blocks.tip: Beware the circumflex: « qu'il fût » (subjunctive) versus « il fut » (passé simple). One accent is the whole difference between two tenses.

passages.title: À la manière d'un moraliste (pastiche original)
passages.french:
Il est un genre d'hommes qui ne parlent jamais d'eux-mêmes et qui, par ce silence même, ne parlent que d'eux.
Ils entrent tard dans une pièce, saluent peu, s'assoient loin de la lampe, et attendent qu'on les prie.
On les prie ; ils refusent ; on insiste ; ils cèdent, et l'on croit leur devoir quelque chose.
J'en connus un, autrefois, qui portait sa modestie comme d'autres portent un titre.
Il fallait, pour obtenir de lui trois mots, qu'on lui en offrît cent.
On le disait profond parce qu'il était lent ; on l'eût dit sage s'il eût été moins soucieux de le paraître.
La Cour, qui juge vite et se corrige rarement, l'admira douze ans sans savoir de quoi.
Il mourut fort estimé, laissant deux maximes, dont l'une était de son frère.
Je ne blâme point ces gens-là : ils occupent la place que notre paresse leur abandonne.
Nous aimons mieux deviner un mérite que le vérifier.
Ce qui coûte à trouver nous semble toujours plus précieux que ce qui s'offre.
Ainsi le mystère tient lieu de talent, et l'ennui de gravité.
Le grand art de ces hommes n'est pas de se taire : c'est de se taire au bon moment.
Quiconque saura cela n'aura plus besoin d'esprit ; il lui suffira d'une bonne montre.
passages.english:
There is a kind of man who never speaks of himself and who, by that very silence, speaks of nothing else.
They come late into a room, greet few people, sit far from the lamp, and wait to be asked.
They are asked; they refuse; one insists; they yield, and one believes oneself in their debt.
I knew one, long ago, who wore his modesty as others wear a title.
To obtain three words from him, one had to offer him a hundred.
He was called deep because he was slow; he would have been called wise had he been less anxious to seem so.
The Court, which judges quickly and rarely corrects itself, admired him for twelve years without knowing what for.
He died much esteemed, leaving two maxims, one of which was his brother's.
I do not blame such people: they occupy the place our own laziness leaves them.
We would rather guess at a merit than verify it.
What costs us effort to find always seems more precious than what offers itself.
So mystery stands in for talent, and boredom for gravity.
The great art of these men is not to keep silent: it is to keep silent at the right moment.
Whoever grasps that will have no further need of wit; a good watch will do.

lessons.title: Réécrire
lessons.description: The same content, rebuilt for a different effect and a different register: cutting, thickening, softening, hardening — and knowing which lever produces which result.

blocks.heading: Réécrire n'est pas corriger
blocks.body: Correcting removes mistakes; rewriting changes the effect. French editorial vocabulary keeps the two apart: « la relecture » hunts errors, « le remaniement » redistributes material, « la refonte » rebuilds from the plan up. Before touching a sentence, decide which of the three you are doing — most bad rewriting is a refonte attempted with the tools of a relecture.

examples.french: La relecture a corrigé douze fautes ; le texte reste illisible.
examples.english: The proofread fixed twelve mistakes; the text is still unreadable.
examples.note: clean does not mean effective

examples.french: Le remaniement a déplacé la conclusion en tête.
examples.english: The reworking moved the conclusion to the front.
examples.note: same material, new order — often the biggest gain for the least effort

examples.french: Après trois moutures, il a fini par tout refondre.
examples.english: After three drafts, he ended up rebuilding the whole thing.
examples.note: « une mouture » = a version, a pass

examples.french: Ce paragraphe ne demande pas d'être allégé, mais étoffé.
examples.english: This paragraph does not need lightening; it needs fleshing out.
examples.note: the two opposite moves: élaguer / étoffer

examples.french: Peaufiner un texte qu'il faudrait réécrire, c'est perdre deux fois son temps.
examples.english: Polishing a text that ought to be rewritten wastes your time twice over.
examples.note: polish last, never first

blocks.tip: Ask what the reader should feel after the paragraph, not what it says. If you cannot answer, no amount of tightening will help.

blocks.heading: Les leviers : sept gestes qui changent tout
blocks.body: Rewriting in French runs on a small number of repeatable moves. Nominalise to make a text abstract and administrative, or de-nominalise to bring it back to life. Move from passive to active to restore an agent. Cut fillers (« il y a », « le fait que », « au niveau de »). Replace an abstract noun with a concrete one. Shorten the sentence, or fuse two into a period. Change the tense. Change the person. Each lever has a predictable effect — learn them singly before combining them.

examples.french: Une décision a été prise par la direction. → La direction a décidé.
examples.english: A decision was taken by management. → Management decided.
examples.note: passive + nominalisation removed: five words saved and an agent restored

examples.french: Le fait qu'il soit parti nous a surpris. → Son départ nous a surpris.
examples.english: The fact that he left surprised us. → His departure surprised us.
examples.note: here nominalisation helps: it kills a heavy subordinate clause

examples.french: Il y a beaucoup de gens qui pensent que… → Beaucoup pensent que…
examples.english: There are many people who think that… → Many think that…
examples.note: « il y a … qui » is the most common filler frame in written French

examples.french: Au niveau du budget, c'est compliqué. → Le budget pose problème.
examples.english: At the level of the budget, it's complicated. → The budget is a problem.
examples.note: « au niveau de » is the classic tic to hunt down

examples.french: Nous constatons une amélioration. → Ça va mieux.
examples.english: We observe an improvement. → Things are better.
examples.note: same information, two registers apart

blocks.tip: Apply one lever at a time and reread. If you pull three at once you will never know which one produced the improvement — or the damage.

blocks.heading: Changer de registre sans changer de sens
blocks.body: Register is not politeness; it is the social distance encoded in the words. French moves between « familier », « courant » and « soutenu » through vocabulary, through syntax (question forms, negation with or without « ne »), and through figures: « la litote » says less to mean more, « l'euphémisme » softens, « l'hyperbole » inflates. The exercise that teaches this fastest is to write the same three facts three times, changing only the register.

examples.french: Familier : Ils ont annulé, on n'a rien pu faire.
examples.english: Casual: They cancelled, we couldn't do a thing.
examples.note: dropped « ne », « on » for « nous »

examples.french: Courant : Ils ont annulé la réunion et nous n'avons rien pu faire.
examples.english: Neutral: They cancelled the meeting and we could do nothing.
examples.note: full negation, explicit object

examples.french: Soutenu : L'annulation nous a privés de tout moyen d'action.
examples.english: Formal: The cancellation deprived us of any means of action.
examples.note: nominalisation + abstract vocabulary = instant elevation

examples.french: Litote : Ce n'est pas un mauvais texte.
examples.english: Understatement: It is not a bad text.
examples.note: in French this normally means it is very good

examples.french: Euphémisme : Il nous a quittés. / Hyperbole : Un désastre absolu.
examples.english: Euphemism: He passed away. / Hyperbole: An absolute disaster.
examples.note: the same event can be softened or inflated without lying about the facts

blocks.tip: Elevation is not about long words. A soutenu text with a familiar syntax sounds pretentious; keep the whole sentence consistent or the register cracks.

blocks.heading: Nominalisation et dénominalisation
blocks.body: Turning a verb into a noun is the main gear-change of French written style. Verb → noun (« il a été nommé » → « sa nomination ») compresses and abstracts, which suits reports, headlines and administrative prose. The reverse move restores agency and movement. Watch the suffixes: -tion, -ment, -ance/-ence, -age, -ure, and the bare deverbal (l'accueil, le rejet, l'appel). Each nominalisation you keep costs the reader an agent.

examples.french: Les prix ont augmenté. → L'augmentation des prix inquiète.
examples.english: Prices have risen. → The rise in prices is worrying.
examples.note: -tion: the fact becomes a topic you can then comment on

examples.french: Le texte a été remanié. → Le remaniement du texte a pris deux mois.
examples.english: The text was reworked. → The reworking of the text took two months.
examples.note: -ment on a verb of process

examples.french: On l'a accueilli froidement. → Son accueil fut glacial.
examples.english: He was received coldly. → His reception was icy.
examples.note: bare deverbal noun — the most compact and the most literary

examples.french: La mise en œuvre de la réforme a échoué. → La réforme n'a pas été appliquée.
examples.english: The implementation of the reform failed. → The reform was not applied.
examples.note: de-nominalising is what makes a bureaucratic text readable again

examples.french: Après vérification, refus. → Nous avons vérifié, puis nous avons refusé.
examples.english: After verification, refusal. → We checked, then we refused.
examples.note: extreme nominal style versus plain verbal style: same facts, opposite effect

blocks.tip: Count the -tion words in your paragraph. Above two, the reader is reading a summary of a text rather than the text itself.

blocks.heading: Atténuer et durcir : les outils de la modalisation
blocks.body: French softens or hardens a statement without touching its content, through modalisation. Softeners: conditional (« il conviendrait »), impersonal framing (« il semblerait que »), hedges (« une certaine », « quelque peu »), litotes. Hardeners: present indicative, deontic verbs (« devoir », « exiger »), intensifiers (« sans réserve », « en aucun cas »), and fronting the demand. The subjunctive after « il faut que », « exiger que » belongs to the hard end; « il serait souhaitable que » to the soft.

examples.french: Il conviendrait de revoir ce paragraphe.
examples.english: It would be advisable to revise this paragraph.
examples.note: maximum softening: conditional + impersonal, no agent named

examples.french: Nous exigeons que ce paragraphe soit revu.
examples.english: We demand that this paragraph be revised.
examples.note: same request at the hard end: named agent + subjunctive

examples.french: Il semblerait que le calendrier ait glissé.
examples.english: It would appear that the timetable has slipped.
examples.note: conditional + subjunctive: the writer refuses to assert

examples.french: Le calendrier n'a pas été tenu.
examples.english: The timetable was not met.
examples.note: flat indicative — a hardening obtained purely by removing hedges

examples.french: Votre analyse n'est pas dénuée d'intérêt.
examples.english: Your analysis is not without interest.
examples.note: double litotes: polite on the surface, decidedly cool underneath

blocks.tip: Never soften twice in the same sentence. « Il conviendrait peut-être éventuellement de… » reads as fear, not as courtesy.

passages.title: Une note de service, trois fois
passages.french:
Le stage de réécriture commençait toujours par le même exercice, et personne n'y échappait.
On distribuait une note de service authentique, dix lignes, sur la fermeture d'un parking.
Première consigne : « Réécrivez-la pour un enfant de dix ans. »
Les stagiaires découvraient alors que le texte, une fois débarrassé de ses nominalisations, tenait en deux phrases.
« Le parking sera fermé lundi. Garez-vous dans la rue. » Rien d'autre n'était vrai.
Deuxième consigne : « Réécrivez-la pour un tribunal. »
Il fallait cette fois nommer les responsables, dater les décisions, écarter tout ce qui n'était pas vérifiable.
Le texte doublait de longueur et perdait son ton d'excuse ; on y voyait enfin qui avait décidé quoi.
Troisième consigne, la plus redoutée : « Réécrivez-la pour ceux qui vont la lire en arrivant, à sept heures, sous la pluie. »
Là, aucune règle ne suffisait plus.
Il ne s'agissait ni d'élaguer ni d'étoffer, mais de savoir ce que l'on devait au lecteur : une excuse, une solution, ou les deux.
Les meilleurs textes de la journée furent les plus courts, et pas un seul ne commençait par « Nous vous informons que ».
À la fin, le formateur relisait les trois versions à voix haute, sans dire laquelle il préférait.
Il répétait seulement, en rendant les copies, que réécrire n'est jamais changer d'avis : c'est changer de destinataire.
Puis il ajoutait, comme s'il s'en excusait, que la plupart des textes illisibles n'avaient tout simplement jamais eu de destinataire du tout.
passages.english:
The rewriting workshop always began with the same exercise, and nobody escaped it.
An authentic internal memo was handed out, ten lines, about the closure of a car park.
First instruction: “Rewrite it for a ten-year-old.”
The trainees then discovered that the text, once stripped of its nominalisations, fitted into two sentences.
“The car park will be closed on Monday. Park in the street.” Nothing else in it was true.
Second instruction: “Rewrite it for a court.”
This time you had to name those responsible, date the decisions, and set aside anything unverifiable.
The text doubled in length and lost its apologetic tone; at last you could see who had decided what.
Third instruction, the most dreaded: “Rewrite it for the people who will read it on arrival, at seven in the morning, in the rain.”
At that point no rule was enough any more.
It was a matter neither of pruning nor of fleshing out, but of knowing what you owed the reader: an apology, a solution, or both.
The best texts of the day were the shortest, and not one of them began with “We hereby inform you that”.
At the end, the trainer read the three versions aloud, without saying which he preferred.
He merely repeated, as he handed back the papers, that rewriting is never changing your mind: it is changing your addressee.
Then he would add, as if apologising for it, that most unreadable texts had quite simply never had any addressee at all.
